title: dot - the debugger
subtitle: A ladybug named Dot who refuses to give you the answer
overview: Ask an LLM a coding question and it hands you a finished, tailored solution — the exact wrong thing when you're trying to learn. Dot answers from real documentation instead, and never bluffs.
body: When you're learning to code, a normal LLM is almost too helpful — ask it anything and it hands back a finished, tailored solution, which quietly kills the learn-by-doing loop. I wanted a small on-screen helper that answers simple doubts — syntax lookups, what an error means, how a loop or a concept actually works — pulled from real documentation. Enough to unstick you and sharpen your thinking, never enough to hand over the answer. And I wanted to do it without a paid LLM API.

It's pure local retrieval, no generative model involved at all. Documentation gets curated into small chunks in a corpus file, each one paraphrased in my own words rather than pasted — that's for licensing as much as anything (cppreference, for instance, is CC-BY-SA; other docs vary, and paraphrasing is the one habit that's safe everywhere). Every chunk gets embedded once with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 via sentence-transformers. At query time, the question gets embedded too, checked against the corpus with cosine similarity, and the nearest chunk comes back. A two-threshold guardrail decides how confident to sound: above the high threshold it answers straight, in the middle band it shows the closest chunk flagged as a best guess, and below the floor it just says it doesn't know yet. It never bluffs.

The interface is a small floating, frameless, always-on-top ladybug — my own pixel art. Click her, type a one-line question, and the answer shows up in a side popover with a bit of fade-and-rise animation.

Retrieval over generation was the point, not a limitation — returning the actual doc snippet, rather than a generated explanation, is the whole anti-spoon-feeding guarantee, since there's no model left to over-explain or leak a full solution. Paraphrasing every chunk does triple duty: better retrieval, teaching-first phrasing, and clean licensing across sources. Building it also taught me that coverage is the corpus — when "for loop" returned the wrong chunk, my instinct was to tune the thresholds, but the actual problem was a missing chunk. The system only knows exactly what I've curated, which keeps it honest and debuggable. No vector database either — at this scale, a plain NumPy dot-product is enough, and deliberately so.
The retrieval engine works end-to-end, and the floating UI is running on my Mac. The first corpus is C++, expanding topic by topic, with Python next.
